title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Page 132 completes Problem 5, adds a Corollary, solves Problem 6, and begins the closing Scholion.

(i) End of Problem 5. The setting is Z = Z(x,y,p,q,r,…,Φ) with Φ = ∫𝔷 dx, where 𝔷 itself depends on Φ through dΦ/dx = 𝔷(x,y,y',…,Φ). The task is to extremize ∫_0^a Z dx. The previous page reduced the first variation to the operator Σ(−d/dx)^k[(Z_k − U 𝔷_k)]. In this sum the multiplier U is defined by U = e^{−∫𝔏}V with V = ∫ e^{∫𝔏} L dx, where V vanishes at x=a. Euler adds that the 'absolute parts' (boundary terms) at x=0 and x=a can each be set to zero to fix the integration constants.

(ii) Corollary. Differentiating V = e^{∫𝔏}U gives dU + U𝔏 dx = L dx with U(a)=0. In modern terms U is the adjoint (costate) variable, U' = −𝔏U + L, ∂Z/∂Φ = L, solved backward from a terminal condition. It is exactly the Lagrange multiplier/costate one gets by treating Φ' = 𝔷 as a differential constraint.

(iii) Problem 6. This is the special case in which the integrand depends on its own running integral: Φ(x) = ∫_0^x Z dx, with Z = Z(x,y,y',y'',…,Φ). The task is to extremize Φ(a). In modern form this is ż = L(t,q,q̇,…,z), extremize z(T); that is Herglotz's generalized variational principle (action-dependent or contact Lagrangians).
- Varying gives (δΦ)' = L δΦ + ω, with ω = Nδy + Pδp + Qδq + Rδr + ….
- Hence δΦ = e^{∫L}∫e^{−∫L} ω dx.
- Integrating by parts with ∫e^{∫L} L dx = e^{∫L}, the term −∫ω cancels the remaining parts. This leaves δΦ(a) = (1/T(a))∫_0^a T ω dx, where T = e^{−∫L dx}.
- Further integration by parts gives the Euler–Lagrange equation TN − (TP)' + (TQ)'' − (TR)''' + … = 0, together with weighted boundary terms.

Expanding with T' = −LT, the first-order case is N − P' + LP = 0, i.e. ∂Z/∂y − d/dx ∂Z/∂y' + (∂Z/∂Φ)(∂Z/∂y') = 0. This is precisely the Herglotz equation (1930). Euler also gives the higher-derivative version and the boundary terms.

(iv) Scholion. Euler stresses that the purely analytic (δ-) method reproduces the results of the 1744 Methodus inveniendi. It also yields the boundary terms that fix constants left undetermined there, i.e. natural boundary/transversality conditions. The next page applies these to the brachistochrone ending on a given curve.
errors: No substantive error. The prefactor 1/T multiplying the variation is a constant, to be evaluated at x=a (with T normalized at x=0). Euler leaves the limits of ∫L dx implicit; this does not affect the Euler–Lagrange equation but matters for the boundary terms.
The closing parenthesis of the first bracket in the displayed variation of Problem 6 is missing in print (typographical).

ideas.what: Costate/adjoint multiplier U for a functional whose integrand contains an auxiliary running integral Φ with Φ' = 𝔷(…,Φ): dU + U𝔏dx = L dx, U(a)=0
ideas.modern_name: Adjoint (costate) equation / Lagrange multiplier for a differential constraint (Pontryagin-type terminal condition)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (multipliers, 1760s–1788); costate formalism: Bolza, Pontryagin et al. 1950s
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744), Ch. III treats integrands containing indefinite integral formulas; repeated analytically here in E297

ideas.what: Extremizing Φ(a), where Φ' = Z(x,y,y',…,Φ): the integrand depends on its own running integral. Euler–Lagrange equation TN − (TP)' + (TQ)'' − … = 0 with T = e^{−∫∂Z/∂Φ dx}
ideas.modern_name: Herglotz generalized variational principle (action-dependent / contact Lagrangians), including the higher-order case
ideas.usually_credited_to: G. Herglotz (1930 lectures); later Guenther, Gottsch, Georgieva and others (1990s–2000s)
ideas.where_published: Possibly in a related form in Methodus inveniendi Ch. III (cases where [Z] contains Π); explicitly here in E297 (1766)

ideas.what: Boundary ('absolute') terms of the first variation used to determine integration constants
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–62) and Euler; standard in the δ-calculus
ideas.where_published: E296/E297 (Elementa calculi variationum and Analytica explicatio), Novi Comm. Petrop. 10 (1766)

missed.claim: Problem 6 is exactly Herglotz's variational principle, ż = L(t,q,q̇,z) with z(T) extremized. Euler derives the Herglotz equation in the integrating-factor form (e^{−∫L_z}L_q)' -type, i.e. TN − (TP)' + … = 0, including higher-order Lagrangians and boundary terms. This was 164 years before Herglotz. The modern contact-mechanics literature credits Herglotz and does not, to my knowledge, cite E297.
missed.quote: Si functio Z ... etiam formulam integralem Φ=∫Zdx inuoluat ... TN − d.TP/dx + dd.TQ/dx² − d³.TR/dx³ + etc. = 0
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Herglotz/contact Lagrangian mechanics (dissipative systems, Noether theorems for action-dependent Lagrangians) is an active area. Euler's integrating-factor form T = e^{−∫∂L/∂z} is the standard device there, so it is a historical priority point.

missed.claim: In the Corollary Euler defines the multiplier U by a linear ODE with a terminal condition at x=a. This is an explicit backward-integrated costate equation for a variational problem with a differential constraint.
missed.quote: dU+U𝔏dx=Ldx ex qua quantitatem U ita definiri oportet, vt ea euanescat, posito x=a
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is an early precursor of adjoint/costate methods in optimal control. The point is mostly historical, and partly already present in the 1744 Methodus.

deep.surprise_reason: Euler's handling of integrands containing indefinite integrals is known from the Methodus (Goldstine discusses Ch. III). However, the clean statement and solution of the self-referential case, i.e. Herglotz's principle with integrating factor and boundary terms, seems not to be credited to Euler in the modern Herglotz/contact-mechanics literature. That is a notable but historical priority point.
transcription_corrections: Problem 6: the image reads 'Φ=∫Zdx' (plain Z, the same function), not 'Φ=∫𝔷dx'. In the solution it reads 'δΦ=δ∫Zdx', also plain Z. This is essential: it is what makes Problem 6 the self-referential case.
First displayed variation in Problem 6: the bracket after 'etc.' is unclosed in the print; the transcription is faithful.
